column3: Names provision from heaven and earth within a wider confession of God's sole governance.
Makes creation, return to earth, and renewed emergence one concrete cycle.
Directly pairs God's origination of creation with its repetition.
The preceding member of the same rhetorical series grounds exclusive deity in answering distress.
The immediate continuation adds exclusive knowledge of the unseen and the coming resurrection.
Extends provision to every creature and places it under God's comprehensive knowledge.
Joins sole creation, provision from heaven and earth, and the denial of any other deity.
Continues the local discussion of doubt about the Hereafter without adding to the focus argument.
Concise restatement of the one agent who originates and restores, already developed more fully above.
An earlier member of the same series ties creation and heavenly water to the exclusion of rivals.
Its image of heaven and earth neither mourning nor granting reprieve does not clarify the focus claim.
Shares the imperative to demand proof for a claim of other deities.
Directly tests alleged partners by whether they can originate and restore creation.
Divine knowledge of what people conceal does not materially develop the focus argument.
Affirms the arrival of a proof, but without the focus's creation or rival-deity test.
Presents origination and restoration as God's own act and links them to supreme authority.
The command to Solomon's addressees does not add to the focus theme.
Provision for those thought dead supplies a specific instance of life continuing beyond visible death.
God maintains heaven and earth and summons people out from the earth.
Uses the first creation as the model and promise for creation's restoration.
Treats spending from God's provision, but only indirectly touches the focus's sustaining provision.
Directly attributes provision from heaven and earth to God, though without the full creation-return test.
Localizes hidden things in a clear record, complementing divine exclusivity only indirectly.
Its exhortation to spend from provision is not a substantial link to the focus argument.
Shows provision as continually dependent on God's release rather than an independent possession.
The punishment rain in the preceding passage does not add to the focus's proof of divine agency.
Depicts provision as part of a particular rescue and strengthening of a vulnerable community.
Combines origination, restoration, and return to God in a single ordered sequence.
Records the local objection to being brought out after becoming dust.
The rejected lexical resonance around the name of Ad is not positive support.
Demands proof for an exclusionary salvation claim, a more limited parallel to the focus challenge.
Tests alleged partners through guidance rather than the focus's creation and provision.
The destruction of the first Ad does not clarify origination, restoration, or provision.
Another member of the local series excludes rivals through guidance and mercy rather than the focus triad.
States the nearby denial of the promised return without supplying its proof.
The historical reference to Ad does not add a useful connection here.
Its generic demand to produce a book is a distant parallel to demanding proof.
The account of the queen's rule does not develop the focus claim.
Identifies the beginning of human creation, supplying one side of the origin-and-return pair.
Connects creation's beginning and restoration with universal return and judgment.
The consolation addressed to the Prophet does not add to the focus argument.
Calls the lasting garden reward a good provision, but in a distinct eschatological setting.
Its challenge over livestock prohibitions does not illuminate the focus claim.
Its description of believers and certainty in the Hereafter is too general here.
Frames provision as lawful and wholesome, without developing its source or proof function.
Another nearby rhetorical question excludes rivals through earth's ordered stability.
Links provision from heaven to reviving dead earth, an observable analogue for renewed life.
Requires each community to bring proof and exposes false claims before God.
The demand to bring ancestors back is a terse challenge around resurrection.
The nearby demand for the promised event supplies the local objection the focus answers.
Contrasts worldly appearance with God's unbounded provision, a peripheral qualification.
Challenges opponents to return the departing soul, marking human inability to restore life.
The account of sun worship is background to the surah but does not add to this proof formula.
Its account of treaty-breaking and conflict is unrelated to the focus's divine-agency argument.
Locates provision and the promise in heaven, reinforcing the focus's heavenly source of sustenance.
Traces creation, heavenly water, fruits, and rivers as a connected provision sequence.
Links received provision to gratitude and worship in a practical but narrower way.
States that invoking another deity lacks proof and leaves the claimant accountable to the true Lord.
The local warning that part of the promised event may be close adds little to the focus claim.
Pairs the beginning with return, though without the focus's explicit rival-deity challenge.
Combines creation, provision, death, life, and the challenge whether any partner can do any of it.
The limit on guiding those who turn away does not develop the focus argument.
Its decisive proof in Joseph's trial is not the evidentiary test posed in the focus.
Challenges alleged deities to show what they created and to supply authoritative evidence.
Heavenly water turning earth green is a partial provision image already represented more fully.
Urges spending from provision before judgment, a secondary ethical consequence.
Calls for observing how creation began and infers the final creation from it.
The command to inspect the fate of criminals does not add to the focus's proof.
Contrasts truth with falsehood by denying falsehood the power to originate or restore.
Names God as creator of heaven and earth and asks for clear authority, but in another dispute.
Shows every creature submitting at the trumpet blast, supplying the event toward which restoration leads.
The rejected lexical association in a list of destroyed peoples is not positive support.
Its contrast between knowing and unknowing worshippers does not clarify the focus triad.
Provision that revives dead land is explicitly made an analogy for coming forth.
Distinguishes worldly provision from final judgment within Abraham's prayer for a town.
Denies partners any comparable creative power and affirms God as creator of all things.
The call to Moses does not materially develop the focus claim.
Its legal provisions for family maintenance are too context-specific to add here.
The challenge to produce a comparable surah is only a general parallel to demanding proof.
States that God provides both dependent creatures and people, widening the focus's provision claim.
Describes a possible return to sea peril, not the creative restoration central to the focus.
Its challenge to produce forged surahs is a remote parallel to the focus's demand for proof.
The image of those unable to hear does not develop the focus argument.
Corrects the inference that restricted provision means divine humiliation, qualifying how provision is read.
Requests a more guiding book as evidence, but does not address rival creative power.
Its contrast of worldly play and the living Hereafter is too general for this argument.
The prohibition and consequences of usury do not add to the focus claim.
Places heaven-and-earth creation alongside the disputed promise of resurrection.
Relates spending from provision to a lasting return, a secondary ethical application.
A particular restoration of Moses's staff illustrates return in a limited sign.
Its rebuke for worldly enjoyment and arrogance does not develop divine origination or provision.
Defends the good provision God has brought forth, but adds little beyond earlier provision texts.
Its discussion of death and attribution of events does not clarify the focus argument.
Attributes control of heaven, earth, and the expansion or restriction of provision to God.
The oath by the earth and its spreading does not add a substantive link.
Describes measured expansion and restriction of provision, already more fully represented above.
Its fasting regulations do not develop the focus's creation, return, or proof challenge.
Makes return to earth and being brought out again an explicit material cycle.
Names the promised day and safety from its great terror, a distant outcome of resurrection.
The immediate provision in Joseph's speech does not contribute to the focus argument.
Sets out death, life, death again, renewed life, and return to God as one comprehensive cycle.
Joins creation of heaven and earth, rain, revived land, creatures, and provision as public signs.
Contrasts God's power to give life and cause death with a human ruler's inadequate claim.
Attributes bringing living from dead and dead from living to God, directly supporting exclusive life-giving agency.
Names God creator of all things and denies any deity besides Him.
States that God originates creation and then returns it, grounding the focus's central pair.
Condenses divine power over life and death and the final return to Him.
Names the maker of heaven and earth and frames created order as signs for those certain of meeting God.
Makes creation and replacement of people depend wholly on God's will.
Affirms creation of heaven and earth in truth and God's transcendence over claimed partners.
Uses water from heaven and earth's revival after death as a direct sign of life-giving provision.
Denies that alleged partners can provide anything from heaven or earth.
Argues from creating heaven and earth to God's ability to create people again.
Links earth's ordered setting, paths, heavenly water, and diverse vegetation as provision.
Connects heaven and earth's formation and water as the source of all living things.
Identifies the Lord as creator of heaven and earth and presents that claim as witnessed testimony.
Traces human creation from earth through death and resurrection, making renewed creation explicit.
States that God gives life to the dead and has power over everything.
Names God as the one who gives life, causes death, and gives life again.
Details successive formation and concludes that God is the best of creators.
Places death after created human life as the next stage of the cycle.
Explicitly completes the preceding human cycle with resurrection on the Day of Rising.
Frames measured water from heaven as provision that God can also remove.
Attributes the creation and diverse movement of every creature to God.
Ascribes creation of everything and its precise measure to God while denying any partner.
Links sent winds and pure water sent down from heaven to divine mercy.
Makes the heavenly water give life to dead land and supply creatures and people.
Records the admission that God created heaven and earth and subjected sun and moon, exposing inconsistency in associating others.
Records the admission that God sends heavenly water to revive dead earth.
Joins the creation of heavens and earth's stability with rain and every kind of creature, then challenges rival makers.
Makes dead earth revived by rain and yielding grain an explicit sign of life and provision.
Confronts the denial of resurrection by recalling human creation from a drop.
Preserves the objection about decayed bones whose answer is supplied by first creation.
Answers that the One who produced bones the first time will give them life again.
Argues from creating heaven and earth to God's ability to recreate people.
Portrays the efficacy of God's command in bringing a thing into being.
Shows God taking souls at death and returning some until an appointed term.
States without qualification that God is the creator of all things.
Uses the greater creation of heaven and earth as evidence against doubting human resurrection.
Names God as the maker of earth and heaven and as the provider of good things.
Traces creation from dust through life and death to an appointed end.
Challenges those who set up equals to the One who created the earth.
Treats revived dead earth after rain as a sign that its giver of life will raise the dead.
Names the originator of heaven and earth and the creator who multiplies creatures.
Attributes the scattering of creatures through heaven and earth to God and affirms His power to gather them.
Records the admission that the Mighty Knowing created heaven and earth.
Attributes the earth's ordered habitation and paths to God.
Links measured heavenly water, revival of dead land, and coming emergence in one analogy.
Questions those who acknowledge God as creator yet turn away from His exclusive claim.
Argues that the creator of heaven and earth can give life to the dead.
Rejects doubt about resurrection by recalling that first creation did not exhaust divine power.
Directs attention to signs in the earth that support the focus's appeal to observable evidence.
Challenges the possibility that people created themselves or are independent creators.
Attributes both death and life to God in a concise exclusive formulation.
Confronts people with God's creation of them and their refusal to acknowledge it.
Invokes knowledge of the first creation to press recognition of restoration.
Attributes dominion, life, death, and power over all things to God.
States God's creation of heaven and earth in truth and His shaping of people.
Calls the earth made tractable by God a place from which people eat His provision.
Describes God causing humanity to grow from the earth.
Challenges the denial that God can reassemble human bones.
Concludes that the creator of male and female is able to give life to the dead.
Recalls human creation from a humble fluid as evidence of originating power.
Directs people to consider their food, opening the following account of its provision.
Attributes abundant poured water to the source of human food.
Pairs the water with earth split open for growth and provision.
Calls people to consider from what they were created.
Names God as the one who creates and proportionates.
Identifies God as the creator at the opening command to recite.
